stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 month old boy admitted overnight with his first episode of coryza followed by wheeze and feeding difficulty. He is exclusively breast fed and is now taking about half his usual volume per feed. His mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy at 39+2 weeks and he has had no previous admissions.

On arrival he is quietly alert with mild subcostal recession, wet cough, wheeze and crackles bilaterally. He has had no apnoeas. He is on room air with continuous SpO2 monitoring.

Over the last hour his oxygen saturations have drifted from 94% to 88% with feeds and 91% at rest. Nasal suction has cleared moderate secretions. Chest signs are unchanged and he is not in extremis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152 /min, respiratory rate 58 /min, SpO2 89% on room air at rest, temperature 37.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Subcostal recession, no head bobbing, no nasal flare, capillary refill 2 s, alert and consolable
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR pending, no chest x-ray performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in oxygen therapy?

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe on room air with hourly checks
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids do not shorten bronchiolitis and are not part of the RCH pathway; the immediate issue is hypoxia which needs oxygen, not steroids. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Escalate directly to heated humidified high flow nasal cannula 2 L/kg/min from room air now
options.rationale: The AU PARIS trial and RCH pathway both make HFNC a second line device after failed low flow rather than the first oxygen chosen; jumping straight to HFNC has not been shown to reduce PICU admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg on oxygen and reassess in twenty minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months as there is no consistent benefit on admission length, oxygen need or work of breathing; salbutamol is not the answer to falling saturations. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; AAP Clinical Practice Guideline 2014)

options.text: Start low flow oxygen 1 to 2 L/min via nasal prongs titrated to SpO2 at or above 90%
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance identifies low flow nasal prong oxygen 1-2 L/min as the first line escalation for infants dropping below the SpO2 target of 90%; humidification and heating are not required at these flow rates. HFNC is reserved for failure of low flow after two hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue room air observation with two hourly nasal suction and repeat saturation in one hour
options.rationale: Persistent SpO2 at 89% at rest is below the RCH target of 90% and mandates oxygen now rather than a further period of observation on room air; ongoing hypoxia risks feed failure and apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: This infant meets RCH criteria for oxygen with SpO2 at 89% at rest and 88% with feeds despite airway clearance. The RCH pathway starts oxygen at low flow via nasal prongs 1-2 L/min with a saturation target of 90%. HFNC is reserved for failure of low flow after two hours, not as an initial device. Neither salbutamol nor systemic corticosteroids alter the natural history of viral bronchiolitis and neither addresses hypoxia.
key_points: SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90%, not 92-94%
First line oxygen is low flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min
HFNC is second line after failed low flow, not first
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months
explanation.pearls: The PARIS trial showed early HFNC does not reduce PICU admission compared with rescue HFNC after low flow failure - low flow first is both cheaper and evidence based.

stem:
You are the paediatric intern seeing a 22 month old boy in the emergency short stay unit at 2 am with two nights of coryza and a barking cough. His mother reports he woke tonight with a hoarse cry and noisy breathing on inspiration.

He is sitting on his mother's lap alert and interactive. He has audible stridor at rest which improves when he settles. There is mild suprasternal recession. Chest is otherwise clear on auscultation with no wheeze or crackles. He drinks water when offered and there is no drooling.

He was fully immunised on schedule and has had no previous croup admissions. There is no history of foreign body inhalation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest that settles when calm, mild suprasternal recession, no cyanosis, colour normal, alert

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose to give now?

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg single dose now with four hours observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is second line to oral dexamethasone when a child cannot tolerate an oral dose; there is no vomiting or refusal here so the oral route is preferred and cheaper. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose now with four hours observation
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved by RCH for severe croup with stridor and marked recession at rest that does not settle, or with agitation or exhaustion; using it for moderate croup gives no added benefit over 0.15 mg/kg. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now with four hours observation
options.rationale: RCH croup guidance uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose for mild and moderate croup, giving effective symptom relief with the lower dose. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. Stridor at rest that settles when calm is moderate. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for three days with GP review tomorrow
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone has weaker evidence than dexamethasone with a shorter duration of action requiring a multiday course, and re-presentation rates in AU emergency data are higher; dexamethasone is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution alone with three hours observation
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup, and a steroid must still be given because adrenaline effect wears off in 90-120 minutes; adrenaline alone risks rebound stridor without underlying anti-inflammatory cover. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: This child has moderate croup on the RCH scoring - stridor at rest that settles when calm with mild recession and no cyanosis or agitation. Both mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; the 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe presentations. Adrenaline is added only to severe or life threatening croup and always with dexamethasone cover. RCH observes for four hours after steroids or three hours after nebulised adrenaline before discharge.
key_points: Mild and moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral single dose
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline
Nebulised adrenaline dose is flat 5 mL of 1:1000, not per kg
Observe for 3 hours after last adrenaline before discharge
explanation.pearls: The 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone dose is often used reflexively - RCH specifies 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup, which covers most emergency presentations.

stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the short stay unit reviewing an 18 month old girl brought in by her father with 24 hours of watery diarrhoea and three episodes of non bilious vomiting. Her older brother had similar symptoms last week that settled. She has been offered clear fluids at home but vomits within ten minutes of each offer and has passed no urine in the six hours prior to arrival.

She is quiet on her father's lap and cries with a few tears. Mucous membranes are dry. Capillary refill is 2 seconds centrally. Her weight three weeks ago at a nurse review was 11.2 kg; today she weighs 10.6 kg.

A single dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg was given on arrival forty minutes ago with brief effect; she has since had one further small vomit after 30 mL of oral rehydration solution.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes with tears, capillary refill 2 s, alert, no abdominal tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Repeat oral ondansetron 4 mg and continue small oral sips of rehydration solution every five minutes
options.rationale: The AU ondansetron dose for a child under 15 kg is 2 mg not 4 mg, and repeat dosing is not recommended in the emergency department pathway; further oral only has already failed once. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert an IV cannula, give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus and continue at full maintenance rate
options.rationale: IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure; in mild to moderate dehydration NGT is preferred and has lower cannulation failure and complication rates in AU emergency populations. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and rehydrate with oral solution at 25 mL/kg in the first hour then reassess
options.rationale: RCH gastroenteritis pathway makes nasogastric rehydration first line when oral trial fails in mild to moderate dehydration (5-10%); it avoids IV access, has fewer complications and equal efficacy in AU trials. Rate is 25 mL/kg in the first hour then continue over 4-6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Admit for observation on continued small oral offers of dilute apple juice every hour by cup
options.rationale: Continued oral trial without route change ignores the failure of the first oral attempt with antiemetic cover, and diluted juice has an inappropriate electrolyte content and osmolality compared with oral rehydration solution. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give loperamide 0.2 mg/kg orally to slow bowel transit and continue oral rehydration solution
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are contraindicated in children with acute infective gastroenteritis due to the risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged infection; they are not part of the AU pathway. (Source: AMH: Antidiarrhoeals)

explanation.summary: This child has 5-6% dehydration with failed oral trial after ondansetron. RCH pathway makes NGT rehydration the next step - it has equivalent efficacy to IV in AU trials with fewer complications, no need for cannulation and shorter time to full rehydration. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure. Antimotility agents like loperamide are contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line when oral fails in mild to moderate dehydration
IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure
Ondansetron dose is banded by weight: 2 mg for under 15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg
Loperamide is contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: The AGREE trial (Melbourne) showed NGT rehydration was non-inferior to IV with fewer complications - AU practice has shifted decisively toward NGT first.

stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 22 month old girl brought by her father with two days of low grade fever and pulling at her right ear. She had one episode of vomiting overnight and has been more irritable than usual but is taking her usual fluids and about two thirds of her normal food. She is fully immunised.

On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is red and bulging with loss of normal landmarks. There is no perforation or discharge. The left ear is normal. She has a clear runny nose and a normal oropharynx with no exudate. Chest is clear. There is no neck stiffness and she is not photophobic.

She has no known drug allergies and has not been given any antibiotics in the previous six months. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and lives at home with parents in Adelaide.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane red and bulging with no perforation, left ear normal, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Amoxicillin clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg/dose twice daily for seven days as first line antibiotic monotherapy
options.rationale: Amoxicillin clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48-72 hours on amoxicillin, or where there is a high concern for beta lactamase producing organisms; it is never first line in uncomplicated paediatric AOM in the AU pathway. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for five days with a return in 48 hours if not improving
options.rationale: Immediate antibiotics are indicated for children under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, systemically unwell children or perforated AOM; a well 22 month old with unilateral AOM does not meet criteria and gains little from immediate treatment. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Analgesia and safety net advice with a delayed antibiotic script to fill only if not improved in 48 hours
options.rationale: RCH and eTG endorse analgesia with delayed antibiotic in non Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children over 6 months without perforation who are systemically well; most cases resolve without antibiotics and delayed scripts reduce use without increasing complications. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute otitis media; eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Topical ciprofloxacin ear drops for seven days without any oral antibiotic and review in one week
options.rationale: Ciprofloxacin ear drops are used for otitis externa or for chronic suppurative otitis media with a perforation; they cannot cross an intact tympanic membrane and have no role in acute otitis media with an intact drum. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Refer to the emergency department for intravenous ceftriaxone and admission for observation
options.rationale: IV antibiotics are reserved for suspected mastoiditis, meningitis or a systemically unwell child not tolerating oral therapy; this child is systemically well with a normal neurological examination and does not need admission. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: The AU approach to uncomplicated AOM in a well child over 6 months is analgesia with delayed antibiotics. Immediate antibiotics are indicated for children under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children (higher risk of chronic suppurative otitis media), systemically unwell children or a perforated ear. When antibiotics are indicated, amoxicillin is first line at 15 mg/kg/dose three times daily for five days; augmentin is reserved for treatment failure.
key_points: Delayed antibiotic script is first line for well non-Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children over 6 months
Immediate antibiotics: under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, unwell, perforated
Amoxicillin is first line; augmentin only after 48-72 h treatment failure
Ciprofloxacin drops are for otitis externa or chronic suppurative OM with perforation
explanation.pearls: The AU rationale for immediate antibiotics in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children is the substantially higher rate of chronic suppurative otitis media and its consequences for hearing and schooling.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3 week old boy in the outpatient jaundice clinic. He was born at 39+4 weeks by normal vaginal delivery to a well mother, birth weight 3.4 kg. His mother reports the whites of his eyes have looked yellow since day 4 and have not improved. She has noticed his stools have become paler over the past week and his nappies now show dark yellow urine that stains.

He is exclusively breast fed, feeding well, and has regained his birth weight plus 200 g. He has no fever and is alert with normal tone.

On examination there is scleral icterus and mild abdominal fullness. The liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin with a firm edge. Spleen is not palpable. Cardiovascular examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 100% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Icterus, liver 2 cm below costal margin with firm edge, no splenomegaly, no petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 168 micromol/L (<26), conjugated bilirubin 42 micromol/L (<15), ALT 82 U/L (<45), GGT 210 U/L (<50), alkaline phosphatase 380 U/L (<450), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2), TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.5-5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day and review the liver enzymes in one month at outpatients
options.rationale: Empirical ursodeoxycholic acid without a diagnosis delays surgical treatment of biliary atresia; UDCA has a role after diagnosis of specific cholestatic disorders but is never a substitute for urgent structural workup. (Source: NASPGHAN 2017)

options.text: Reassure about breast milk jaundice and review the infant in the community clinic at six weeks of age
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and cannot explain a conjugated fraction of 42 micromol/L or pale stools; labelling this as breast milk jaundice delays workup for biliary atresia beyond the 60 day Kasai window and worsens outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence phototherapy on the day ward and repeat total bilirubin measurement in six hours after light exposure
options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to a water soluble form; it has no effect on conjugated bilirubin and can cause bronze baby syndrome in cholestatic infants. This infant has cholestasis, not unconjugated jaundice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Urgent referral to paediatric hepatology for HIDA scintigraphy and intraoperative cholangiogram within one week
options.rationale: A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total in an infant over 2 weeks mandates urgent hepatology workup for biliary atresia; the Kasai portoenterostomy has a much higher success rate if done before 60 days of life. Pale stools plus dark urine with a firm liver make biliary atresia the leading concern. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN 2017)

options.text: Order abdominal ultrasound and repeat conjugated bilirubin measurement in one month in community clinic
options.rationale: An ultrasound is a helpful adjunct but a normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia and a one month delay would push definitive surgery past the 60 day Kasai window when outcomes fall sharply; urgent referral is required regardless of the ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any infant with jaundice beyond 14 days needs a split (conjugated and unconjugated) bilirubin. A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is always pathological and mandates urgent hepatology assessment for biliary atresia. Pale stools, dark urine and a firm liver support this. The Kasai portoenterostomy has a much higher rate of biliary drainage restoration if performed under 60 days of age, and each week of delay reduces success. Do not send this child home on watchful waiting.
key_points: Conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is always pathological
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes fall sharply after 60 days of age
Phototherapy has no role in conjugated jaundice
Pale stools and dark urine are red flags for biliary obstruction
explanation.pearls: The stool colour chart in the RCH resources should be given to every family with prolonged neonatal jaundice - parents can catch progression to biliary atresia earlier than any single blood test.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7 month old boy admitted with six days of persistent fever above 39 degC that has not responded to paracetamol. His mother reports he has been miserable and off his feeds. He had a red rash on his trunk on day three that has faded. His hands looked puffy yesterday.

On examination today he is irritable with bilateral non exudative conjunctivitis and dry cracked red lips. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Hands and feet show mild oedema without desquamation. A chest x-ray on admission was normal. Blood and urine cultures at 48 hours are negative. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone was started three days ago with no improvement.

He has no known allergies and no significant past history. He was fully immunised at 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172 /min, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctivitis without exudate, cracked lips, no lymphadenopathy, hand and foot oedema, systolic flow murmur
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), platelets 620 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 18.4 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 145 mg/L (<5), ALT 68 U/L (<45), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis 30 white cells per HPF with no growth on culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram and give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high dose aspirin now
options.rationale: Six days of fever plus two of five classical features and multiple supportive laboratory findings (albumin below 30, sodium below 135, platelets rising, sterile pyuria, anaemia, raised ALT) meets the AHA algorithm for incomplete Kawasaki disease with more than three lab criteria. Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin without waiting for full classical criteria to prevent coronary aneurysms. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement; RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Continue ceftriaxone for a further 48 hours pending viral PCR results and clinical reassessment
options.rationale: Delaying treatment beyond day 10 of illness sharply increases the risk of coronary aneurysm; empirical antibiotics without response and negative cultures should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, not further watchful waiting. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg/day for three days as first line monotherapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are added to IVIG only for high risk patients (Kobayashi score high risk, under 12 months in Japanese cohorts) or for IVIG resistance; monotherapy corticosteroids are not first line and IVIG is still required. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and start empirical intravenous aciclovir for suspected HSV encephalitis
options.rationale: There is no seizure, focal neurology or altered consciousness to raise concern for HSV encephalitis, and the clinical and laboratory picture fits incomplete Kawasaki; empirical aciclovir does not address the coronary risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Discharge home on paracetamol with outpatient paediatric review in one week after clinic booking
options.rationale: A miserable infant with six days of unremitting fever, incomplete Kawasaki features and rising markers cannot be discharged; missed Kawasaki disease can cause life threatening coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when there are five or more days of fever with only two or three classical features plus supportive laboratory findings. This child has bilateral non exudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips and extremity oedema plus six supportive lab features. Under the AHA algorithm this warrants IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin. Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply after day 10 of illness so treatment cannot wait for classical criteria. Echocardiography is done at diagnosis and repeated at 1-2 weeks and 4-6 weeks.
key_points: AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria: fever with 2-3 features plus supportive labs
Supportive labs: albumin below 30, sodium below 135, sterile pyuria, anaemia, raised platelets, raised ALT, raised WCC
Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin without waiting for full features
Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply beyond day 10 of illness
explanation.pearls: Infants under 12 months present most often with incomplete Kawasaki and have the highest coronary aneurysm rate - a low threshold for IVIG in this group is life saving.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 5 year old girl brought in by ambulance 90 minutes ago after her first known peanut exposure at a friend's house. Within ten minutes of eating a peanut butter biscuit she developed urticaria, facial swelling and audible wheeze.

Paramedics gave a single intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram at the scene with rapid resolution of wheeze and improvement in tachycardia within five minutes. On arrival she was well perfused with clear chest and no stridor. She received a second intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram in the department 30 minutes ago after a brief return of wheeze, again with prompt response.

She has been observed for 90 minutes since arrival with no further symptoms. She is now bright and alert, drinking water, and has passed urine. Her parents have arrived with her ASCIA action plan blank and her EpiPen Jr script filled.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 102/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, chest clear, no urticaria, no facial swelling, no stridor, no wheeze

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discharge plan from this presentation?

options.text: Admit overnight for a supervised peanut challenge in the paediatric ward the following morning
options.rationale: Deliberate re-exposure to the trigger after an anaphylactic reaction is contraindicated and would not be done as an inpatient challenge; if food challenge is needed it is done later in a supervised immunology setting after negative testing. (Source: ASCIA food allergy guidelines)

options.text: Discharge now with an EpiPen Jr and GP follow up next week to complete the anaphylaxis action plan
options.rationale: ASCIA specifies a minimum observation of four hours after the last adrenaline dose in a child needing more than one dose; discharging at 30 minutes exposes the child to a missed biphasic reaction without adrenaline access at hospital. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

options.text: Admit for 24 hours of hourly observations and oral prednisolone daily for three days as inpatient
options.rationale: A 24 hour admission is not required after a first anaphylaxis that has responded well; oral prednisolone does not reduce biphasic reactions and is not recommended in ASCIA guidance. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

options.text: Observe to four hours after the last adrenaline dose then discharge with ASCIA plan and immunology referral
options.rationale: ASCIA guidance requires a minimum of four hours observation after the last adrenaline dose in a child who had more than one dose or persistent symptoms; the 30 minute mark from the second dose is short of that. Immunology referral is standard for a first anaphylactic reaction to identify the trigger. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024; RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Start an oral antihistamine for three days and dispense an EpiPen 300 microgram for future emergency use
options.rationale: This child weighs 18 kg so the correct device is EpiPen Jr 150 microgram (10-20 kg band); EpiPen 300 microgram is for children 20 kg and above. Antihistamines relieve urticaria but have no role in the immediate anaphylaxis pathway. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends observation for a minimum of four hours after the last adrenaline dose for children who required more than one dose, had persistent or protracted symptoms, or had features suggesting a biphasic reaction. This child had two doses and needs a further 3.5 hours of observation. On discharge every child needs an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan, a prescription for a weight banded adrenaline autoinjector (EpiPen Jr 150 microgram for 10-20 kg, EpiPen 300 microgram for 20 kg or more) and referral to a paediatric immunology or allergy service.
key_points: Observe a minimum of 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose if 2 or more doses needed
EpiPen Jr 150 mcg for 10-20 kg; EpiPen 300 mcg for 20 kg or more
Oral prednisolone does not reduce biphasic reactions
First anaphylaxis warrants immunology referral to identify the trigger
explanation.pearls: Antihistamines and steroids have never been shown to reduce biphasic anaphylaxis - they treat urticaria but do not replace observation time or adrenaline.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar four hours into managing a 9 year old girl admitted with new onset type 1 diabetes and severe diabetic ketoacidosis. She weighs 26 kg. Initial venous pH was 7.02 with bicarbonate 6 mmol/L and glucose 32 mmol/L. She received a single 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus for shock and has been on a fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour with 0.9% saline plus 20 mmol/L potassium chloride at a rate calculated for a 48 hour rehydration with a 5% fluid deficit.

Her glucose has fallen to 14 mmol/L on the four hour blood gas and 5% dextrose was added to the fluids one hour ago. She was drowsy but rousable on admission, GCS 14. Fifteen minutes ago the nurse called you because she has become more difficult to rouse and has vomited once. Her father says she now has a headache.

On assessment she is disoriented, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), pupils 4 mm and equally reactive. Blood pressure has risen from 100/62 to 128/74 and pulse has fallen from 128 to 94.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94 /min (was 128), blood pressure 128/74 mmHg (was 100/62), respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Investigations at 4 h: Venous pH 7.22, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, glucose 14 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L (was 132), potassium 4.2 mmol/L, corrected sodium rising through resuscitation
data_table.Neurological examination: GCS 12 with vomiting and headache, pupils 4 mm equal and reactive, no focal weakness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.15 units/kg/hour and give a further 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus now
options.rationale: Increasing insulin and giving further boluses worsen cerebral oedema by lowering osmolality and dropping glucose too fast; the presenting problem is not persistent acidosis but neurological deterioration during resuscitation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give hypertonic 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes, elevate head 30 degrees, halve fluids and call PICU
options.rationale: Drowsiness, headache, vomiting, hypertension with relative bradycardia (Cushing response) four hours into DKA fluids in a child under 12 with severe presentation defines clinical cerebral oedema; treatment is hyperosmolar therapy (hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg 2.7% or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), head elevation, fluid restriction to 2/3 maintenance and immediate PICU involvement. (Source: BSPED/ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline 2020; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct the acidosis and improve conscious state fast
options.rationale: Bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk and is contraindicated except for life threatening hyperkalaemia; it will not reverse the neurological deterioration and may worsen it. (Source: ISPAD 2022; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT head to exclude intracerebral haemorrhage before starting any osmotic therapy today
options.rationale: Clinical cerebral oedema is a treat first diagnosis - CT is often normal early and delays hyperosmolar therapy; the child should be treated on clinical grounds and imaged only if she stabilises or the diagnosis is unclear. (Source: BSPED/ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline 2020)

options.text: Stop dextrose from the fluids and reduce insulin infusion to 0.05 units/kg/hour at current fluid rate
options.rationale: Reducing insulin without addressing the raised intracranial pressure does not treat the cerebral oedema, and stopping dextrose risks rebound ketosis; the priority is hyperosmolar therapy and PICU escalation, not a tweak to insulin. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Clinical cerebral oedema complicates 0.5-1% of paediatric DKA episodes and has a mortality of about 20% with major morbidity in survivors. Risk factors present here include age under 12, new onset, severe acidosis on admission and a rapid rise in corrected sodium. The Muir criteria triad of headache, vomiting and altered conscious state with Cushing response (hypertension and relative bradycardia) mandates immediate hyperosmolar therapy - hypertonic saline 2.7% at 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg - alongside head elevation, halving the fluid rate and PICU escalation. Do not delay for imaging.
key_points: Diagnose cerebral oedema clinically, treat before imaging
Hyperosmolar therapy: 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes OR mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Reduce fluid rate to two thirds maintenance, head up 30 degrees
Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except for life threatening hyperkalaemia
explanation.pearls: The classic warning is a rise in blood pressure with a fall in heart rate during DKA resuscitation - it is a Cushing response and not a sign the child is recovering.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a rural birth suite ten minutes after the vaginal delivery of a term 3.6 kg baby to a 32 year old G2P2 woman with a labour lasting seven hours. Third stage was actively managed with oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery and the placenta appeared complete after controlled cord traction at eight minutes.

Estimated blood loss is now 900 mL of fresh red loss with clots. On examination the fundus is soft and above the umbilicus. A rapid inspection of the vagina and cervix shows no lacerations and the perineum is intact. She is talking to you and holding her baby but says she feels lightheaded.

Her antenatal blood pressure was consistently 145/95 without medication and she was investigated for chronic hypertension. She has no known drug allergies. IV access has been secured with a wide bore cannula, bloods including group and hold are drawn and 500 mL of Hartmann's is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus above the umbilicus, placenta complete on inspection, no genital tract laceration, perineum intact
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 10 units IM given at delivery, ongoing oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 hours in progress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to give?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram with fundal massage and continued oxytocin infusion currently running
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia or cardiac disease because of the risk of hypertensive crisis, stroke and myocardial ischaemia; this woman has documented chronic hypertension. (Source: AMH: Ergometrine)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram with fundal massage, repeat every 15 minutes to maximum eight doses
options.rationale: RANZCOG stepwise PPH management gives ergometrine as second line, then carboprost when ergometrine fails or is contraindicated by hypertension; a history of chronic hypertension makes ergometrine contraindicated so carboprost is the appropriate second line uterotonic here. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; eTG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Bimanual uterine compression alone and reassess in 15 minutes without additional pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Bimanual compression is a temporising manoeuvre used alongside pharmacological escalation for ongoing PPH; using it in place of additional uterotonic wastes time and does not address the uterine atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as the only additional pharmacological therapy given now
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid should be given for any PPH over 500 mL within three hours as an adjunct, not instead of a second line uterotonic; the atony must be treated pharmacologically at the same time. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device without giving any additional pharmacological uterotonic
options.rationale: Intrauterine balloon tamponade is second line after failure of medical management and preparation for theatre; pharmacological escalation to a second uterotonic is appropriate before mechanical intervention in a stable woman with atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: Uterine atony causes the majority of primary PPH. RANZCOG stepwise pharmacological escalation is fundal massage, oxytocin (given), ergometrine (contraindicated by chronic hypertension), carboprost, then misoprostol. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given for any PPH over 500 mL within three hours of birth as an adjunct. Bimanual compression and balloon tamponade are used if medical measures fail. Do not give ergometrine in hypertensive, pre-eclamptic or cardiac disease.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia or cardiac disease
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth for any PPH over 500 mL
Bimanual compression and balloon tamponade are used with, not instead of, pharmacology
explanation.pearls: The AMH warns that ergometrine and combination Syntometrine can precipitate hypertensive crisis in eclamptic women - remember to check the antenatal blood pressure before reaching for the ampoule.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 28 year old G1P0 at 34+2 weeks referred by her GP for elevated blood pressure and a severe frontal headache that started this morning. She has had two episodes of blurred vision and mild right upper quadrant discomfort since arrival.

Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 with normal booking bloods. Home readings over the past week have run 138-148/88-96. She is on no regular medications and reports no allergies.

On admission her blood pressure is 168/108 mmHg confirmed on repeat reading with a size appropriate cuff. Urinalysis shows 3+ proteinuria with a spot protein creatinine ratio of 65 mg/mmol (<30). CTG is reassuring at 145 bpm baseline with normal variability. She is neurologically alert with brisk reflexes and no clonus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 168/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC, foetal HR 145 /min
data_table.Examination: Alert, brisk reflexes without clonus, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, no peripheral oedema documented
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90), ALT 152 U/L (<45), urate 0.44 mmol/L (0.14-0.34), LDH 380 U/L (<250)

lead_in: Alongside intravenous labetalol for blood pressure control, what is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, plus antenatal betamethasone
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms and HELLP features (platelets under 100, ALT over 70) requires magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis (Magpie trial protocol) alongside blood pressure control and betamethasone before delivery planning. AMH uses the AU spelling magnesium sulfate. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023; RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy statement)

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin loading 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis with oral maintenance postnatally
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is the evidence based seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia (Magpie trial) with clear superiority over phenytoin; phenytoin is not first line and gives worse outcomes. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

options.text: Nifedipine 10 mg orally as sole antihypertensive and admit for observation without seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: This woman meets criteria for severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP features and neurological symptoms and requires magnesium sulfate; a blood pressure agent alone leaves her unprotected against eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

options.text: Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia without corticosteroids or magnesium loading dose
options.rationale: Delivery is planned but stabilisation with magnesium sulfate and antihypertensives comes first, and at 34+2 weeks betamethasone should be given if delivery can be safely delayed for 24 hours; skipping stabilisation increases maternal and neonatal risk. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg intravenous now and reassess her neurological state and reflexes in one hour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are used to abort an active eclamptic seizure only if magnesium fails; they cause maternal sedation and respiratory depression and have no role in prevention. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: This woman has severe pre-eclampsia at 34+2 weeks with cerebral symptoms (headache, blurred vision), HELLP features (platelets 92, ALT 152, LDH raised) and blood pressure well over the severe threshold of 160/110. Management is simultaneous control of blood pressure with IV labetalol or hydralazine, seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate per the Magpie protocol, and antenatal corticosteroids as delivery is planned within 24-48 hours after stabilisation. Delivery mode is determined by cervix and foetal status; caesarean is not automatic.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia criteria: BP 160/110, HELLP, neurological symptoms, or end organ dysfunction
Magnesium sulfate load 4 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/hour infusion (Magpie protocol)
Monitor magnesium clinically: reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output
Betamethasone if delivery may be delayed 24-48 hours between 24 and 34+6 weeks
explanation.pearls: The AU spelling is magnesium sulfate (INN in AMH), not sulphate - and magnesium toxicity is monitored clinically, not by routine serum levels.
